Simplified form of 邊.  Phonosemantic compound with two sound components and two meaning components. 辶 and 方 represent the meaning, while 自 and 丙 represent the sound. The traditional component 自 was removed for simplification. The traditional component 丙 was removed for simplification.
Simplified from 邊 (臱 → 力). Officially adopted as the simplified form of 邊 in the Chinese Character Simplification Scheme (《漢字簡化方案》) in 1956.

walk
Phonosemantic compound with two sound components and two meaning components. 辶 and 方 represent the meaning, while 自 and 丙 represent the sound.

Originally 臱. Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *mpeːn): semantic 辶 (“walking; movement”) + phonetic 臱 (OC *men). The semantic component 辵 (now 辶) was added during bronze inscriptions.
Perhaps cognate with 偏 (OC *pʰen, *pʰens, “side; oblique”), 片 (OC *pʰeːns, “partial; one-sided”), 諞 (OC *ben, *brenʔ, *benʔ, “glib-tongued; insincere”) (Schuessler, 2007).
Based on Old Vietnamese data, Gong (2019) proposes the additional preinitial *tə- to the Baxter-Sagart reconstruction.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Character Database), CUHK
evidence.field: 形義通解 / bronze form and early uses
evidence.text: The database describes bronze 邊 as containing 辵, 自, 丙, and 方. It reports an analysis attributed to 張世超 in which 自 and 丙 both function as sound elements, and 方 contributes the sense ‘side’; it gives ‘beside’ as the original meaning. It cites the bronze inscriptions 大盂鼎 for a use meaning ‘frontier region’ and 散氏盤 for the place-name 邊柳. These are source assertions; the multiple-phonetic-element analysis differs from accounts that assign a single phonetic element.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese Character Database), CUHK
evidence.text: The page quotes the Han-era Shuowen account: 邊, ‘行垂崖也’ (walking by a precipitous edge), ‘from 辵, sound from 𦤝,’ with fanqie 布賢切. It separately records Guangyun fanqie 布玄 and places 邊 in the level-tone 先 rhyme, grade IV, labial initial. Shuowen’s explanation is a historical lexicographic account, not independent proof of the graph’s original composition.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫

evidence.field: 古文字 / sound series / Old Chinese reconstructions
evidence.text: The entry presents a sequence of Shang, Western Zhou, Warring States, and Shuowen forms and identifies 臱 as 邊’s sound-series member. It gives Zhengzhang Shangfang (2003) Old Chinese 臱 *men and 邊 *mpeːn; in Baxter–Sagart (2014) it gives Middle Chinese ‹pen› and Old Chinese *pˁe[n]. The differing reconstructions belong to distinct systems and should not be collapsed into a single pronunciation. The entry also says the oracle-bone form consists of 自 and 丙, which may both be phonetic; that proposal differs from the bronze analysis assigning 方 a semantic role.
evidence.title: 邊 - 维基词典，自由的多语言词典

evidence.source: 教育部《異體字字典》 (Taiwan Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants)
evidence.field: 說文释形, standard form, pronunciation, senses, cited examples
evidence.text: This dictionary records 邊 as the standard form, quotes Shuowen’s ‘行垂崖也。从辵，𦤝聲’ and gives Mandarin biān. Its senses include a boundary/frontier, beside or bank, side/edge, limit, direction, and ‘while’ in the paired construction 邊…邊…. It supplies examples attributed to classical works and later texts, including a Tang poem for ‘frontier,’ and cites Shuowen, Yupian (‘塞也’), and Guangyun (‘邊陲也’). The page provides a lexicographic sense history, but the examples shown do not establish the first date or a continuous path for each extension.
evidence.title: 邊 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.field: 隸書 and dated graphic specimens
evidence.text: The page lists labeled specimens of 邊 from Western Han manuscripts and maps, Eastern Han inscriptions, Qin slips, and a Western Jin brick, and explains clerical transformation generally as a shift from seal-script rounded strokes toward angular strokes. The inspected text gives specimen labels and dates, but does not itself expose all glyph images as text; no image-based shape comparison was made.
evidence.title: 邊的字源字形

evidence.source: 中华人民共和国教育部
evidence.text: The search result for the Ministry’s page states that the State Council scheme was to take effect in stages and that the first table of 230 simplified characters became standard for printed and written documents from 1956-02-01. The Ministry page itself timed out when opened, so this date is a search-result claim and has not been verified against inspected page contents here.
evidence.title: 国务院关于公布汉字简化方案的决议(1956年)

evidence.field: 形義源流通解; bronze composition and cited contexts
evidence.text: The database reports a bronze form composed of 辵, 自, 丙, and 方. An analysis attributed to 張世超 treats 自 and 丙 as sound elements and 方 as contributing ‘beside’; the database gives ‘beside’ as the original sense. It cites 大盂鼎 for a use meaning a frontier region and 散氏盤 for the place-name 邊柳. These are the database’s analysis and readings of cited contexts, not an independently checked reading of the artifacts. The same page quotes Shuowen’s Han-era analysis ‘行垂崖也。从辵，𦤝聲’ and its fanqie 布賢切; Guangyun is separately listed with 布玄 and level-tone 先, grade IV, labial initial. Shuowen is a historical dictionary analysis, not proof of original composition.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫

evidence.field: 古文字; phonetic series and paleographic analysis
evidence.text: The entry presents Shang, Western Zhou, Warring States, and Shuowen forms, labels 臱 a same-sound-series member, and gives Zhengzhang Shangfang (2003) Old Chinese 臱 *men and 邊 *mpeːn. It gives a different system, Baxter–Sagart (2014), with Middle Chinese ‹pen› and Old Chinese *pˁe[n]. These reconstructions are system-specific and cannot be merged. Its account proposes that the oracle-bone form contains 自 and 丙, possibly both sound elements; for the bronze form it lists 辵, 自, 丙, 方, with 辵 and 方 possibly semantic and 自 and 丙 phonetic. It says the small-seal lower-right part of 𨘢 reflects a corruption of 方. The article also reports Schuessler’s proposed cognates 偏, 片, 諞; this is a disputed lexical proposal, not a demonstrated graphic or semantic chronology.
evidence.title: 邊 - 维基词典，自由的多语言词典

evidence.text: The page indexes forms labeled as oracle-bone, bronze, Chu manuscripts, Qin slips, small seal, and clerical examples. It labels particular clerical specimens to Western Han, Eastern Han, Qin, and Western Jin contexts, including slips, maps, steles, and a brick. The page’s accompanying account describes clerical change generally as replacing rounded seal strokes with angular strokes. This indexed page establishes candidate examples and labels, not a verified line-by-line glyph comparison.
evidence.title: 邊的字源字形

evidence.field: File description and licensing for 邊-bronze.svg
evidence.text: Commons describes this as a vector depiction of 邊 in bronze-script style, 300×300 SVG. Its file history records an upload by Justinrleung on 2017-07-18 and component metadata; it is a modern digital redraw, not a photograph or facsimile of an ancient bronze. The description releases the SVG representation to the public domain. The page does not identify a particular dated artifact as the source of this glyph, so its period is only broadly ‘bronze-script style’ and its precise inscription provenance is not established.

context.provenance: Base evidence consists of imported local JSONL excerpts. Source names identify upstream datasets; extraction may lose sense and language boundaries. Further external evidence and research activity are documented separately in the dossier.
editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

gaps: The inspected authoritative pages do not establish whether the earliest form was already 邊 or whether an earlier 臱 graph was the direct ancestor; Wiktionary labels 臱 as original, but the opened evidence does not settle that claim.

The formation accounts conflict: Shuowen treats 辵 as semantic and 𦤝/臱 as phonetic; CUHK reports a bronze analysis with 自 and 丙 phonetic and 方 semantic; Wiktionary says the oracle form has 自 and 丙 and that they may be phonetic. The sources inspected do not resolve which component analysis best explains the earliest forms.

No component has been assigned an origin_form here because the consulted descriptions do not establish the required form-to-component relationship as a chronological ancestor or full positional form. Modern shape resemblance alone does not establish this.

The proposal that 自 and 丙 mark sound does not independently establish their ancient pronunciations as used in this graph; no separate primary phonological analysis of both elements was inspected. The database gives Old Chinese reconstructions for 邊/臱 via Wiktionary, but not a directly comparable reconstruction for 自 and 丙 in this compound.

No independently dated earliest attestations for each meaning or documented chronological chain from ‘beside/edge’ to ‘frontier,’ ‘direction,’ or the ‘while’ construction were established. The database reports specific bronze-inscription contexts, but the inspected page does not date those inscriptions in the displayed text.

The simplified-form dossier claim that 边 was officially adopted in 1956 is broadly compatible with the Ministry search-result summary, but the Ministry page could not be opened and the exact entry for 邊→边 was not verified in an inspected primary scheme document.
The external pages inspected did not substantiate the dossier’s modern readings across Cantonese, Japanese, Korean, and Vietnamese. Only Mandarin biān was verified in the opened Taiwan dictionary.
The primary bronze inscription images and relevant manuscript images were not visually inspected; the account relies on the pages’ textual descriptions and catalog labels.

The inspected sources offer differing analyses of the earliest composition: Shuowen assigns 辵 semantic and 𦤝 phonetic; the CUHK account attributed to 張世超 identifies 自 and 丙 as sound elements and 方 as semantic; Wiktionary describes the oracle form as 自 plus 丙 and the bronze form as 辵, 自, 丙, 方. The present research does not resolve which proposal best explains the earliest form.

A proposed phonetic role for 自 and 丙 is not independently validated here by comparable, source-specific ancient reconstructions for each component in this graph. The existence of reconstructions for 邊 and 臱 alone does not establish the sound of the depicted or borrowed names of the component shapes.

No securely dated first occurrence for each sense, nor a documented continuous semantic chain from ‘beside’ to ‘frontier’, ‘boundary’, direction, or the paired ‘while’ construction, was established. CUHK reports bronze contexts for frontier and a place-name but this inspection did not independently date or verify the inscriptions.

The database’s claimed bronze component roles and readings are source assertions; artifact images and inscription contexts were not independently examined here. No chronology is inferred from the listed glosses.

The proposed Commons oracle-style redraw lacks verified reuse terms and specific artifact provenance in the inspected result, so it is not proposed as a reusable glyph item. The bronze-style redraw is a modern reconstruction whose precise specimen source is not given.

No primary inscription photograph or manuscript glyph with checked, reusable rights and verified identity was established in this search. The broad graphic sequence is supported by dictionary indexes, but not by direct visual comparison.

The searched pages inspected here do not verify the 1956 official adoption details for 边; the prior Ministry page access failure remains unresolved. The exact entry in a primary simplification scheme was not checked.
Modern Mandarin and Cantonese readings were found in the opened secondary entry; other dossier readings for Japanese, Korean, and Vietnamese were not independently verified in this research pass.

The direct image URLs could not be opened by the web tool. Their path was obtained from the Commons file-description result, not guessed, but actual downloadability was not verified here. The acquisition failure may reflect the tool’s access restriction; retain the bronze redraw only as a sourced candidate, subject to the harness download check.

The Commons search result provides public-domain terms for both redraws, but the oracle redraw has no specific artifact provenance in the inspected description. Neither candidate should be described as a photograph or as a glyph visually inspected by this researcher.

Direct image retrieval failed: Commons Special:FilePath requests were inaccessible through the web tool, and the previously supplied hash-directory upload paths were not confirmed by the inspected pages. Do not use those guessed paths; harness download must independently resolve the direct image URL from the verified Commons source page.

The bronze-style redraw cites Hanziyuan B02283 but does not pin the glyph to a particular dated inscription. The oracle-style redraw cites Xiaoxuetang but does not identify a specific bone or date. The silk redraw points to Sinica image 51.EA4A and label 曾172, but the manuscript image itself was not opened here.
The file descriptions and licenses establish candidates and reuse provenance only. No glyph pixels were inspected; these are explicitly redraws, not artifact photographs.
